query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of hafnium (around 0.5 atomic percent) to equal‐atomic NbMoTaW will induce a controlled formation of a ductile, metastable Hf‐rich second phase (likely with an hcp structure) within the predominantly bcc matrix. This dual‐phase microstructure will promote transformation‐induced plasticity (and/or twinning) at room temperature, increasing ductility, while preserving the high-temperature bcc strength and maintaining irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal‐atomic NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy, exhibiting a single-phase body-centered cubic (bcc) structure with excellent performance at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of hafnium (targeting ~0.5 at%) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Performance assessed at room temperature (for ductility), at high temperature (around 1600 °C for strength), and under irradiation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a limited, metastable Hf-rich secondary phase (likely adopting a hexagonal-close packed structure) that is dispersed inside the bcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Hf addition locally destabilizes the bcc lattice at room temperature, leading to the nucleation of a ductile Hf-rich phase that can accommodate deformation via transformation-induced plasticity and/or twinning. Because the volume fraction remains low, the bcc matrix (which confers high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance) is preserved at elevated temperatures and under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the Hf-modified alloy is expected to show significantly improved room-temperature ductility (increased strain to failure) while retaining similar high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: The untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with single-phase bcc structure and poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on keeping the Hf addition low (around 0.5 at%) to avoid excessive phase segregation or formation of unwanted phases that could degrade high-temperature strength or irradiation performance. Processing conditions must ensure that the bcc matrix remains dominant at high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact nature, fraction, and stability of the Hf-rich phase at room temperature and under irradiation require experimental validation, and the optimum Hf content might need fine tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of NbMoTaW alloys with varying hafnium additions (e.g., 0, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%). Characterize the microstructure (via XRD and TEM) to confirm the presence and morphology of any Hf-rich phases. Then perform room-temperature tensile tests, high-temperature (around 1600 °C) mechanical tests, and controlled irradiation experiments. Compare the mechanical properties and irradiation-induced defect evolution to the baseline NbMoTaW alloy.
measurements: Microstructural phase analysis (phase fraction and morphology)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (a) the hafnium addition fails to produce a measurable improvement in room-temperature ductility, (b) the high-temperature performance or irradiation resistance degrades relative to the baseline alloy, or (c) the microstructural analysis does not reveal the formation of a minor, metastable Hf-rich phase.

Significantly Improving the High-Temperature Tensile Properties of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1 Alloys by Microalloying Hf

Abstract: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. Phase-transition assisted mechanical behavior of TiZrHfTax high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Recent developments of high-entropy alloys with high strength and high ductility draw attention to the metastability-engineering strategy. Using first-principle theory, here we demonstrate that reducing the Ta level in the refractory TiZrHfTax system destabilizes the body-centered cubic (bcc) phase and leads to the appearance of the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phase embedded in the bcc matrix. The alloying-induced features of the elastic parameters for the cubic and hexagonal structures are mapped out in details, and strong sensitivity to the crystal lattice and chemistry is revealed. Results show softening of the bcc matrix with decreasing Ta concentration which ensures ductile behavior. However, the elastically nearly isotropic hcp precipitates possess enhanced resistance against shear which promotes strengthening of the TiZrHfTax dual-phase system. The present atomic-level insight provides strong evidence to the experimental observation, and emphasizes the significance of quantum-design for advanced multi-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent strength-ductility combinations.

The Effect of Scandium on the Structure, Microstructure and Superconductivity of Equimolar Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractIn this study, we investigate the scandium-containing Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr system of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Using the arc-melting method, we synthesized nine equimolar alloys (five 4-, three 5- and one 6-component), with all of them containing Sc. The alloys were characterized by XRD, electron microscopy and EDS, while superconductivity was investigated via electrical resistivity, specific heat and the Meissner effect. The results were compared to the parent Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory HEAs, forming a single-phase body-centered cubic (bcc) structure and quite homogeneous microstructure. The addition of Sc produces a two-phase structure in the Sc-Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys, with one phase being bcc and the other hexagonal close-packed (hcp). The hcp phase absorbs practically all Sc, whereas the Sc-poor bcc phase is identical to the bcc phase in the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr parent system.
